week_headline: Green tea 'fat-melting' claims surge across European health news, promising weight loss without diet or exercise

top10.claim: Trucul de slăbit cu ceai verde : Secretul care topește grăsimea fără diete și fitness
top10.verdict: Green tea does contain catechins (especially EGCG) and caffeine, which can give a small, real nudge to metabolism — but the effect is modest, roughly 3-4% increase in energy expenditure, and it absolutely does not 'melt fat' on its own without diet or exercise. The framing of a secret trick that replaces healthy habits is misleading and not supported by the clinical evidence. Think of green tea as a gentle, pleasant addition to a healthy lifestyle, not a shortcut around one.
top10.verdict_highlight: No drink replaces diet and movement
sources: Hursel R et al., International Journal of Obesity, 2009 — meta-analysis on green tea catechins and weight loss
Phung OJ et al., Journal of the American Dietetic Association, 2010
NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health — Green Tea fact sheet
European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) — Opinion on green tea catechins, 2018
top10.global_opinion: In Japan, green tea is deeply embedded in daily culture and consumed primarily for pleasure and tradition, not marketed as a weight-loss tool — the hype framing would feel unusual there. In the US and UK, green tea extracts are sold as diet supplements, though regulators like the FDA and NHS have cautioned that high-dose supplements can carry liver risks. In Romania and broader Eastern Europe, where this headline originates, sensationalist 'secret trick' health content is a known pattern in online media, often targeting people frustrated with slow progress.
top10.brit_take: A nice cup of green tea is a genuinely lovely habit — just don't expect it to do your squats for you.
